documents.title: Community Benefits Agreement (posted by the City as a draft; signature pages blank)
Sabin Center: Community Benefits Agreements and Data Center Development

community_fund.controlled_by: Foundation fund: a committee of the City's Director of Community Planning and Economic Development, one representative from each of two owner entities, an EDC Lancaster County board member, a Lancaster County Community Foundation representative, and a mayoral appointee confirmed by Council. City fund: the City, in consultation with the owners.
community_fund.notes: $10M to the Lancaster County Community Foundation economic development fund and $10M to the City's Sustainable Development and Clean Energy Fund, paid in $2.5M installments tied to construction financing and operations start of the two East campus units. Secured by a $20M letter of credit or a guarantee from an entity with $100M net worth. The $250,000 strategic-plan payment is credited against the $10M, so the total is $20M, not $20.25M as some summaries say. No payment schedule is written for the Harrisburg Pike building. Committee meetings are not public.

sources.quote: shall be credited against any amount required by 8.1.1

clawbacks.notes: The City gave no tax incentives, so there is nothing to claw back. The closest instrument is a $10M contingent clean energy letter of credit: if a building's power contract falls short of clean-energy thresholds the owner pays $2.5M to $10M per building, and below 60 percent clean the City can seek injunctive relief up to discontinuance of operations.

decommissioning.notes: An e-waste management plan is required and tenant equipment must be removed on decommissioning, but there is no bond, escrow, or site-restoration fund.

grid_costs.notes: The agreement is silent on transmission and substation cost. Press reports the developer partners intend to fund about $200M of PPL Electric grid improvements including a new substation. That commitment lives outside the CBA.

water.notes: Hard cap of 20,000 gallons per day of municipal water per campus, closed-loop cooling with no added chemicals. The prior printing plant used 100,000 to 125,000 gallons per day. The annual report to Council covers clean energy only; water use is not reported.

sources.quote: shall not exceed twenty thousand (20,000) gallons per day

noise.measured_at: Nearest residential or park-zoned receivers. The standard is pre-construction ambient (lowest one-hour LEQ, day and night), not a number.
noise.notes: Magnetic-bearing chillers and sound-attenuated generator enclosures required. Generator testing daytime only, never Sundays or federal holidays. Certified noise mitigation plan due within 60 days, post-construction testing required. The City may demand a compliance re-check on complaint only once every two years. 100-foot buffers along streets and residential edges, 50 feet elsewhere.

jobs.notes: The agreement says approximately 150 people at each campus. Local hiring is a good-faith effort with percentage goals to be set in a plan that had not been released as of April 2026. No prevailing wage; only a worker-misclassification clause. Press figures range from 70 full-time at launch to 350 permanent.

local_contracting.notes: No local subcontracting requirement and no road repair term. Owners reimburse City emergency-response costs above $25,000 per incident. Press reports $149M in contracts awarded with over half to local firms, which is practice, not obligation.

transparency.notes: The agreement is a public record under Pennsylvania's Right-to-Know Law with carve-outs for proprietary and security submissions. Owners must keep a public website and complaint portal and report to Council each April on clean-energy percentage and sourcing. The only audit right written runs the other way: the owners may audit the two funds annually. Residents are not third-party beneficiaries and cannot enforce the agreement. Fund committee meetings are not public.

tax.notes: No tax breaks, including no LERTA abatement, and no PILOT. The City received about $7.8M in permit fees and a $327,345 transfer tax.

criticisms.summary: Lancaster Stands Up received the agreement two days before the vote, asked for a seat at the table, and got no response; developers would not accept changes.
Only the City can enforce the agreement. Residents affected by noise cannot sue under it.
Negotiation began after the zoning opinion and demolition permit had issued, so leverage was already spent.
The clean-energy penalty structure was described by a resident as pay to pollute.
